I ran a Hyrox PR with an average heart rate of 145 bpm and all it took was consistent aerobic training.

Leading up to my Hyrox, I was training for a marathon as well, and aerobic training became a huge focus in my prep. Easy runs, long runs, and building my aerobic base taught my body how to work efficiently for long periods of time without constantly redlining.

When race day came for Hyrox, I wasn’t fighting my heart rate the entire time. I was able to stay controlled, recover quicker between stations, and keep moving without hitting the wall.

A lot of people think HYROX is just strength and suffering, but having a strong engine changes everything. The stronger your aerobic base, the harder you can work while making it feel easier.

caption:
Cut my HYROX sled pull from 4:25 → 3:19 and the fix was WAY simpler than you think:

Stop dropping the rope after every pull.

Every time you let go, you create slack and lose
tension = wasted energy + wasted time. Staying
connected to the rope the entire time keeps the sled moving and makes every pull more efficient.

It’s a simple yet effective technical change that makes a huge difference for your Hyrox race.

#hyrox #sledpull #coaching

caption:
3 things that took my HYROX time from 1:13 ➡️ 1:04 — and exactly how I trained them ⬇️

1. Multiple speed sessions every week ⚡️ 
Most people only run at an easy pace and wonder why race pace feels impossible.

What helped me most:
• 1 interval day (ex: 8 x 1K at faster than race pace) 
• 1 threshold/speed endurance day (ex: 7km tempo or broken tempo runs) 
• Running on tired legs after strength sessions

Once I improved my actual speed, my HYROX pace stopped feeling like survival mode.

2. Practice transitions under fatigue 🔥 
Hyrox rewards athletes who can settle their breathing and move efficiently while exhausted.

What I changed:
• Running straight into stations without extra rest 
• Practicing quick transitions in training instead of standing around recovering 
• Doing compromised running (ex: sled push → immediate run)

This alone can save minutes over the course of a race.

3. Build fatigue-resistant strength 💪 
I stopped training like a powerlifter and started training for repeatable output.

What worked best:
• Longer functional intervals 
• High-rep sled work under fatigue 
• Wall balls and lunges when already exhausted 
• Strength circuits with minimal rest

The goal isn’t just being strong. 
It’s staying strong for the entire race.

Most people train Hyrox to finish. 
The fastest athletes train to hold intensity the whole way through.

One thing I’ve been thinking about lately:

A lot of people spend their lives waiting for the perfect moment.

Waiting until they’re more confident.
Waiting until they know exactly what to do.
Waiting until they have more time, more money, more support, or less fear.

But what if that perfect moment never comes?

The thought of reaching the end of my life and looking back with regret scares me far more than failing ever could.

Not because I tried and fell short.
Not because I made mistakes.
But because I never gave myself the chance to see what was possible.

You don’t need all the answers.
You don’t need a perfect plan.
You don’t need to do it alone.

You just need to start.

Because the biggest risk isn’t failure—it’s spending your life wondering what could have happened if you had the courage to begin.

I stopped breathing randomly and started syncing my breath to my steps.

Here’s how:
• Easy runs → inhale 3 steps, exhale 3 steps
• Moderate runs → inhale 2 steps, exhale 2 steps
• Hard runs → inhale 2 steps, exhale 1 step
• Focus on a full exhale (that’s the key)

Why it works:
✔️ Lowers heart rate
✔️ Improves oxygen exchange
✔️ Keeps effort controlled instead of panicked

You’re not out of shape — your breathing is just out of sync.

caption:
I dropped my burpee broad jump time from 3:22 to 2:19 in 10 weeks, and it wasn’t by just doing more burpees.

1. It wasn’t more volume. It was better execution.

I stopped wasting energy. My burpees got tighter, smoother, and more consistent. No extra movement, no standing up fully between reps.

2. I trained fatigue, not fresh reps.

Most people practice burpee broad jumps fresh. In races, you’re never fresh. I trained them after hard efforts - sleds, runs, ski, row - so my body learned to hold form under fatigue.

3. Breathing & rhythm were the game changer.

Once I locked in my breathing and rhythm, everything clicked. Exhale on the drop, controlled breath on the jump. I stopped redlining halfway through the station.

4. Conditioned the station, not just the movement.

This station is about engine + efficiency. I built aerobic capacity around high-rep burpees instead of treating them like a strength movement.

If burpee broad jumps blow up your race, stop doing more - start doing them smarter.

caption:
HERE’S HOW I DID IT:

1. Key workouts I did for a 1:30 half marathon: 
✅ Long Runs (16-22 km)
	•	Run them 20-40 sec per km slower than race pace (4:40-5:00/km).
	•	Include fast finishes (last 3-5 km at goal pace).

✅ Tempo Runs (6-10 km at 4:15-4:20/km)
	•	Improves lactate threshold and helps sustain race pace longer.
	•	Example: 2 km warm-up → 6-10 km at 4:15-4:20/km → 2 km cool-down.

✅ Speed Work (Interval Training)
	•	Boosts your ability to run faster efficiently.
	•	Example workouts:
	•	6-8 x 800m at 3:50-4:00/km (equal rest time)
	•	3-4 x 1.6 km (1 mile) at 3:55-4:10/km (90 sec rest)

✅ Race Pace Runs
	•	Once every 2 weeks, hold 4:15-4:20/km for 10-13 km to get comfortable at race pace.

(Aim for 4-5 runs per week with a mixture of easy runs, speed work, and long runs.)

2. Strength & Mobility Work (3-4x per week)
	•	Focus on core, glutes, and leg strength to prevent injuries.
	•	Exercises like deadlifts, lunges, step-ups, and ESPECIALLY one legged movements.

3. My Race Day Strategy for a 1:30 Half Marathon
✅ Pacing Plan:
	•	KM 1-5: Ease into goal pace (4:17-4:20/km).
	•	KM 6-16: Maintain steady effort (~4:15/km).
	•	KM 17-21.1: Push hard and finish strong!

✅ Nutrition & Hydration:
	•	Take in 30-60g of carbs per hour (gels, chews, or sports drinks).
	•	Drink water every 3-5 km to avoid dehydration.

4. ENJOY IT. All the hard work happens during your training, race day is where you have fun. You got this. 💪🏼

#run #marathontraining #runners
